newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean shipping firms to see '97 earnings rise.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean shipping firms to see '97 earnings rise.

text.p: Strong sales growth and falling costs are likely to lift earnings for South Korean shipping firms this year, but low freight rates and overcapacity in the container business could cap profits, analysts said on Monday.
Fuel oil and operational costs are expected to decline, while sales turnover is forecast to climb, they said.
"The revenue growth will rise thanks to vessel capacity expansions last year," said Sohn Soo-yeon, transportation analyst at ING-Baring Securities.
Jee Hun-seok, a Daewoo Securities analyst, said: "Cheaper fuel oil prices and plans to cut operation costs will help companies trying to reduce expenses."

The industry suffered a huge decline in earnings last year, mainly because of oversupply in the container shipping market. According to Dongbang Peregrine Securities, the industry lost an average of 97 percent in net profits last year from 1995.
The Korean won's steep eight percent depreciation against the dollar last year underscored the shipping sector's heavy exposure to foreign debt.
This year's forecast rise in earnings will partially recoup the losses in 1996, the analysts said.
They said the foreign currency translation loss is likely to be less of a burden this year with the won's depreciation slowing.
But shipping freight rates are expected to stay in a slump this year, putting a cap on the industry's profit growth.
Freight rates for container shipping, which constitute most of the nation's shipping business, are approximately 15 percent lower now against their peak in 1994, the analysts said.
"The container shipping market is expected to remain depressed until early 1998 due to massive new delivery of vessels," said Sohn of ING-Baring.

Container shipping capacity is expected to grow faster than demand in 1997 and 1998, on a jump in shipbuilding orders in 1994 and 1995. From 1998, new capacity should expand more slowly than demand and help reduce surplus capacity.
Bulk shipping freight rates are likely to fare better, although a significant rise is not expected this year due to fleet overcapacity.
"If the supply of new bulk carriers declines and more oil ships are scrapped, bulk freight rates could recover in 1998," said Park Shin-gyu, a shipping analyst at Ssangyong Investment Securities.
Two listed shipping lines, Hyundai Merchant Marine Co Ltd and Hanjin Shipping Co Ltd, and unlisted Choyang Shipping Co Ltd dominate the industry, which is the world's sixth largest.

ING-Baring's Sohn said she expected Hyundai, the largest Korean shipping company in terms of capacity and revenue, to post 28.2 billion won ($31.6 million) in net profit on turnover of 2.6 trillion this year. This compares with a 19.5 billion won profit on 2.1 trillion in sales last year.
Dongbang Peregrine Securities expects Hyundai's earnings to rise to 34.5 billion won on 2.7 trillion in sales.
Prospects for Hanjin, which relies heavily on container shipping, are also rosier this year, the analysts said.
Jee of Daewoo Securities forecast a 14.9 billion won net income for Hanjin on 2.27 trillion in turnover versus a 9.0 billion won profit on 2.05 trillion in turnover in 1996.
Dongbang Peregrine expected Hanjin's profit to rise to 22.8 billion won on 2.32 trillion in sales.
